name: product-launch
description: Takes something built and gets it into the market — tiering the launch to match what it actually warrants, sequencing internal readiness before external announcement, preparing sales and support to answer the questions it creates, choosing the date for a reason, and measuring adoption rather than announcement reach. Use this to plan a launch, right-size one that is consuming more than it deserves, work out why a released feature nobody uses was launched loudly, or run the weeks after launch day.
---

# Product launch

A launch is not an announcement. The announcement is the cheapest part and the part most likely to
be mistaken for the whole thing, which is how features get press coverage and no adoption.

## Tier the launch before planning it

Not everything deserves the same treatment, and treating everything as major is how a team burns
its own attention and its audience's.

- **Tier one** — changes the story you tell about the product, or opens a new segment. Full
  motion: positioning work, press, sales enablement, customer communication, campaign.
- **Tier two** — meaningful to existing customers, not a new story. In-product announcement,
  documentation, a note to affected accounts, sales briefing.
- **Tier three** — improvement. Release notes and nothing else.

Agree the tier before work starts, and expect the pull toward tier one from whoever built it.
Effort spent above the tier is taken from somewhere else, usually from the next launch.

## Sequence internal readiness ahead of the announcement

The order matters and gets reversed constantly. Support and sales find out from the announcement,
then spend launch week answering questions they were never briefed on, badly.

Before anything external: documentation exists, support can answer the top questions, sales knows
who it is for and who it is not for, pricing and packaging are decided and configured, and the
thing works for the accounts that will try it first.

**Have someone outside the team use it from scratch.** The team cannot see the first-run experience
any more, and the first-run experience is what everyone else gets.

## Decide who it is for, and say who it is not for

A launch aimed at everyone lands on no one. Name the segment, the problem it solves, and what
changes for them — and say explicitly who should not use it yet. Sales will otherwise sell it to
whoever asks, and the earliest customers will be the worst-fit ones.

## Pick a date for a reason, and defend the criteria over the date

Launch dates get set by an event, a quarter, or a promise. Whatever fixes it, write down the
criteria that must hold to launch on it — quality bar, documentation, support readiness — and treat
those as the real gate.

**Launching before support readiness is the most expensive way to save a week.** The cost lands as
a bad first impression on exactly the customers most interested in the thing.

## Plan the days after, not just the day

Most launch plans end on launch day, which is where the work starts. Schedule the follow-through:
a second wave for people who missed the first, in-product prompts for users who have not tried it,
outreach to accounts that fit, and a check on the questions arriving in support.

Watch the first support tickets closely. They are the fastest signal about what the launch got
wrong, and they arrive before any dashboard moves.

## Measure adoption, not announcement

Reach, impressions and press mentions measure the announcement. What matters is whether the
intended people are using the thing and whether it did what the roadmap claimed.

Decide the number before launch — how many of which accounts, doing what, by when. A launch
evaluated on engagement metrics chosen afterward is always a success and teaches you nothing.

## Sources

`references/sources.md` in this skill lists the outside authorities that settle the questions
here — what each one is authoritative for, and what you may do with it. Check them before
answering on anything they cover, and cite what you used. Most are free to read and not free
to reproduce; the use note on each is binding.

## Never

- Announce externally before support and sales can answer the obvious questions.
- Run a tier-one motion for a tier-three change because the team is proud of it.
- Launch to everyone because narrowing the audience feels like reducing the impact.
- Report launch success in reach when the goal was adoption.

name: release-and-deployment
description: Ships changes safely and often — pipelines, deployment strategies, feature flags, rollback, and database changes. Use this to design a deployment pipeline, reduce release risk, roll out a risky change gradually, plan a schema migration, or work out why releases are infrequent and frightening.
---

# Release and deployment

Release risk is dominated by batch size. Large infrequent releases are dangerous because many changes
land at once and nobody can tell which one broke it — so teams release less often, which makes each
release larger. The loop is the problem.

## Separate deploy from release

Deploying code and exposing behavior to users are different acts, and coupling them forces every
deployment to be a business decision.

Decouple with flags: deploy continuously, expose deliberately. This makes rollback a configuration
change rather than a redeployment, which is the difference between seconds and minutes at the worst
possible time.

Flags are inventory and rot. Give each an owner and a removal date; a codebase full of stale flags
has combinatorial states nobody has tested.

## The pipeline is the quality gate

Automate everything between commit and production, and let the pipeline reject. Manual steps get
skipped under pressure, which is exactly when they matter.

Order gates fast-to-slow so failure is cheap: lint and unit tests, then integration, then anything
requiring a deployed environment. A pipeline slow enough to be circumvented is worse than a fast one
with fewer checks, because it will be circumvented.

Build once and promote the same artifact through environments. Rebuilding per environment means the
thing you tested is not the thing you shipped.

## Roll out gradually

Expose to a small population first and watch real signals before widening. Canary or percentage
rollout turns a total failure into a contained one.

Define the abort condition **before** starting, with a threshold and a named decision-maker. Under
pressure, and with the change fresh, the instinct is always to wait a little longer and see.

## Database changes are the asymmetric risk

Code rolls back; data does not. Make schema changes backward-compatible and multi-step: add the new
structure, write to both, migrate, switch reads, then remove the old — with the application tolerant
of both shapes throughout.

Test the migration against production-scale data. A migration that is instant on a development
dataset can lock a large table for a length of time nobody modeled.

## Sources

`references/sources.md` in this skill lists the outside authorities that settle the questions
here — what each one is authoritative for, and what you may do with it. Check them before
answering on anything they cover, and cite what you used. Most are free to read and not free
to reproduce; the use note on each is binding.

## Tooling

Pipelines: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, Buildkite, Jenkins, and similar.

Continuous delivery and progressive rollout: Argo CD, Flux, Spinnaker, and similar; feature flags
for decoupling deploy from release — LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Split, and similar.

Schema migrations: Flyway, Liquibase, Alembic, and similar. Whichever you use, the property that
matters is that migrations are versioned, ordered, and applied by the pipeline rather than by a
person with a database client.

## Never

- Couple deploying code to exposing behavior.
- Promote a different artifact than the one that was tested.
- Begin a rollout without a defined abort condition.
- Ship a schema change that requires the application and database to deploy simultaneously.

    browser engine's own English sentence, which is what the previous three releases
    did for the user, site and 망 구분 forms — with one difference that changes the
    shape of the fix. This is the only one of the four whose commonest failure never
    reaches the server. The 「JSON Schema」 칸 is five rows of free text and the save
    mutation evaluates `JSON.parse(form.schemaText)` inside `mutationFn`
    (AdminPage.tsx:3709), so one stray character makes V8 throw before the request
    is built; react-query catches that synchronous throw and puts it in
    `save.error`, where the Alert printed `Unexpected token '}', "{"properties": }"
    is not valid JSON`. The screen has three free-text boxes and the engine's text
    names none of them. That the throw happens before any request was not inferred
    from the library's source but measured in a real browser against the production
    bundle: zero POSTs reached the server after 「저장」 on broken JSON. The failures
    that did reach the server were the same story — upsertEventDefinition
    (admin.go:1395-1446) answers INVALID_MODE in English and DEFINITION_SAVE_FAILED
    with `err.Error()`, so pgx's own text travelled to the browser. A new
    describeEventDefinitionError in web/src/pages/adminErrors.ts decides the
    guidance, names the box the reader has to fix, and an unknown code still falls
    back to the server's message. The JSON syntax branch sits *before* the switch on
    purpose: that error carries no `code`, so a switch on the code alone drops it
    into the default branch and hands the engine's English straight back. The test
    is `error instanceof SyntaxError`; the `/JSON/` message pattern is only a second
    layer and is guarded by the absence of a code, so a server refusal whose message
    happens to contain "JSON" is not intercepted — asserted rather than assumed.
    DEFINITION_SAVE_FAILED deliberately names no cause: six different places answer
    with that one code (Begin, the INSERT, the version lookup, two Execs, Commit),
    and the INSERT selects the site by `site_key`, so a site_key matching nothing
    inserts zero rows and arrives as pgx.ErrNoRows, indistinguishable from an
    outage. Calling it an already-registered event would be plainly false whichever
    it was: the INSERT carries `ON CONFLICT(site_id,name) DO UPDATE`, so a repeated
    name is absorbed rather than refused. No cause was reproduced against a database
    here, so none is named. The server's text is not deleted — it stays as the
    detail caption, the only clue left to pass on. Kept separate from
    describeUserError, describeSiteError and describeNetworkError for the reason
    those are separate from each other: this handler answers its own set of codes
    and the field to correct is its own. Only `refusal` is shared, so the four paths
    cannot come to read the same input differently; the shared sentences

name: Offline image release
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]
  # A tag push can go unscheduled during a platform incident, and a release that
  # was missed then could not be produced afterwards: the only trigger was the
  # push itself, which does not repeat. This accepts the tag to build.
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      tag:
        description: Tag to build and release, for example v0.31.6
        required: true
permissions:
  contents: write
jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      # The tag being released, from the dispatch input when there is one and from
      # the pushed ref otherwise, so the steps below need no branching.
      #
      # Deliberately not named GITHUB_REF_NAME: the runner sets its own value for
      # the reserved variables regardless of what a job declares, so shadowing it
      # produced a run whose env block displayed the tag while the shell saw
      # "main" and tried to release a tag by that name.
      RELEASE_TAG: ${{ inputs.tag || github.ref_name }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          # A dispatched run starts from the default branch, so the tag has to be
          # checked out explicitly or the image would be built from main.
          ref: ${{ inputs.tag || github.ref }}
      # The commit comes from the tree that was checked out, not from GITHUB_SHA.
      # For a tag push they are the same. For a dispatch — which is how a missed
      # or half-published release is repaired — GITHUB_SHA is the branch the
      # workflow was dispatched against while the checkout above is the tag, so
      # the artifact was stamped with a commit it does not contain. Measured on
      # v0.33.7: the tag's own run reported 2a90aee80a9e and a dispatched rebuild
      # of the same tag reported b1216bf9052b, which is a commit that came after
      # it. The version endpoint exists so an operator can say what they are
      # running; a commit from another branch is worse than none.
      - name: Read the commit being released
        run: echo "RELEASE_COMMIT=$(git rev-parse --short=12 HEAD)" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      # The image is named repository:tag and the archive is one word — the two
      # shapes an operator meets, kept deliberately parallel: momento:v0.34.2
      # loads out of momento-v0.34.2.tar.gz.
      - name: Build service image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --build-arg VERSION="${RELEASE_TAG#v}" \
            --build-arg COMMIT="${RELEASE_COMMIT}" \
            --build-arg BUILD_TIME="$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" \
            -t "momento:${RELEASE_TAG}" .
      - name: Export offline image only
        run: |
          docker save "momento:${RELEASE_TAG}" | gzip -9 > "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz"
          sha256sum "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz" > "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz.sha256"
      # The artifact is the product for an offline deployment, and until now
      # nothing had ever loaded one and started it. This runs the archive that is
      # about to be published — not the image still in the local daemon — through
      # the install sequence the release notes give, so a tarball that cannot
      # start is never published.
      - name: Smoke test the offline artifact
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          # Loading from the archive is the point: it proves what a user receives.
          docker image rm "momento:${RELEASE_TAG}" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
          gzip -dc "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz" | docker load
          sha256sum -c "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz.sha256"

          docker network create momento-smoke
          docker run -d --name smoke-pg --network momento-smoke \
            -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=smoke -e POSTGRES_DB=momento postgres:17-alpine
          for _ in $(seq 1 40); do
            docker exec smoke-pg pg_isready -U postgres >/dev/null 2>&1 && break
            sleep 2
          done

          docker run -d --name smoke-app --network momento-smoke -p 127.0.0.1:8099:8080 \
            -e MOMENTO_POSTGRES_DSN='postgres://postgres:smoke@smoke-pg:5432/momento?sslmode=disable' \
            -e MOMENTO_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN='admin@example.com' \
            -e MOMENTO_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD='smoke-test-password-long-enough' \
            -e MOMENTO_ENCRYPTION_KEY="$(head -c 32 /dev/urandom | base64)" \
            "momento:${RELEASE_TAG}"

          # Ready means the migrations ran and the database is reachable, which is
          # the part an operator cannot verify from the outside.
          ready=""
          for _ in $(seq 1 60); do
            if curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8099/health/ready | grep -q ready; then
              ready=yes
              break
            fi
            sleep 2
          done
          if [[ -z "$ready" ]]; then
            echo "::error title=Offline artifact does not start::/health/ready never answered"
            docker logs smoke-app || true
            exit 1
          fi

          # The archive has to be the version it is named after.
          reported=$(curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8099/api/v1/version)
          echo "version endpoint: $reported"
          if ! echo "$reported" | grep -q "\"version\":\"${RELEASE_TAG#v}\""; then
            echo "::error title=Wrong version in artifact::expected ${RELEASE_TAG#v}, got $reported"
            exit 1
          fi
          # And the commit it names has to be the tag's own, whichever trigger
          # built it. A rebuild of an old tag that reports today's branch head
          # sends anybody investigating to code the image does not contain.
          if ! echo "$reported" | grep -q "\"commit\":\"${RELEASE_COMMIT}\""; then
            echo "::error title=Wrong commit in artifact::expected ${RELEASE_COMMIT} for ${RELEASE_TAG}, got $reported"
            exit 1
          fi

          # The console is embedded in the binary, so a missing build would show
          # up here rather than in any API check.
          curl -fsS -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8099/
          # And the operator's first action has to work.
          curl -fsS -o /dev/null -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8099/api/v1/auth/login \
            -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
            -d '{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"smoke-test-password-long-enough"}'
          echo "offline artifact started, reported ${RELEASE_TAG}, served the console and accepted the bootstrap login"
      - name: Collect smoke test logs on failure
        if: failure()
        run: docker logs smoke-app 2>&1 | tail -50 || true
      - name: Remove smoke test containers
        if: always()
        run: |
          docker rm -f smoke-app smoke-pg >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
          docker network rm momento-smoke >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
      # Publishing has to be repeatable, because the reconciliation workflow exists
      # to repeat it. It dispatches this workflow for a tag whose release is
      # missing or has only one of its two assets — and `gh release create` fails
      # outright when a release already exists, so the half-published case it was
      # written to repair could never be repaired: every dispatch died on "a
      # release with the same tag name already exists" and left the release as it
      # found it. The same error turned a healthy release red whenever
      # reconciliation happened to look while the tag's own run was still
      # building.
      - name: Publish GitHub release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          if [[ -f ".github/release-notes/${RELEASE_TAG}.md" ]]; then
            NOTES=(--notes-file ".github/release-notes/${RELEASE_TAG}.md")
          else
            NOTES=(--generate-notes)
          fi
          if gh release view "$RELEASE_TAG" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "::notice title=Release exists::$RELEASE_TAG is already published; uploading the artifacts in place."
            gh release upload "$RELEASE_TAG" \
              "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz" \
              "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz.sha256" \

              "momento-${RELEASE_TAG}.tar.gz.sha256" \

name: Release reconciliation

# A tag push is a one-shot trigger. Twice now a platform incident dropped it, and
# the result was a tag with no release that nobody would notice without looking:
# the tag is there, the version is announced, and the artifact an offline install
# needs does not exist. This reconciles the two on a schedule, so a missed release
# repairs itself instead of waiting to be discovered.
on:
  schedule:
    # Hourly, off the hour: the top of the hour is when scheduled jobs queue up
    # across GitHub and get delayed the most.
    - cron: "23 * * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  # Needed to dispatch the release workflow for a tag that is missing one.
  actions: write

jobs:
  reconcile:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
        with:
          # Tags are the input to this job, so a shallow clone is not enough.
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: Repair tags with no release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          now=$(date +%s)
          repaired=0
          # Newest first, and only recent tags: an old tag without a release was a
          # deliberate choice by then, and rebuilding it would be surprising.
          while read -r tag created; do
            [[ -z "$tag" ]] && continue
            age_days=$(( (now - created) / 86400 ))
            if (( age_days > 7 )); then
              break
            fi
            # A tag pushed in the last half hour is probably being released right
            # now: its own run builds an image and smoke tests the archive before
            # publishing, so for a few minutes the release genuinely does not
            # exist yet. Dispatching then produced a duplicate run that raced the
            # real one, and one of the two ended red on a release that was fine.
            # Nothing is lost by waiting — this runs every hour.
            age_minutes=$(( (now - created) / 60 ))
            if (( age_minutes < 30 )); then
              echo "$tag was pushed ${age_minutes}m ago; its own release run has not had time to finish."
              continue
            fi
            assets=$(gh release view "$tag" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --json assets --jq '.assets | length' 2>/dev/null || echo "missing")
            if [[ "$assets" == "2" ]]; then
              continue
            fi
            if [[ "$assets" == "missing" ]]; then
              echo "::warning title=Release missing::$tag has no release. Dispatching the release workflow."
            else
              # A release with the wrong number of assets is a half-finished run:
              # the archive and its checksum are published together or not at all.
              echo "::warning title=Release incomplete::$tag has a release with $assets assets, expected 2. Dispatching the release workflow."
            fi
            gh workflow run "Offline image release" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --ref "${{ github.ref_name }}" -f tag="$tag"
            repaired=$((repaired + 1))
          done < <(git for-each-ref --sort=-creatordate --format='%(refname:short) %(creatordate:unix)' 'refs/tags/v[0-9]*')

          if (( repaired == 0 )); then
            echo "Every tag from the last seven days has a complete release."
          else
            # Not a failure: the repair was dispatched and the next run verifies it.
            echo "::notice title=Releases dispatched::$repaired tag(s) were missing a complete release."
          fi
name: CI
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  # A push does not always get scheduled — a platform incident can drop the run
  # while leaving the release workflow to report a startup failure — and without a
  # manual trigger there is no way to verify a commit after the fact.
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # The analytical reports build SQL by hand, so the suite runs them against a real
    # PostgreSQL instance. A syntax or type error there is invisible to unit tests.
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:17-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ci
          POSTGRES_DB: momento
        ports: ["5432:5432"]
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U postgres -d momento"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 3s
          --health-retries 20
    env:
      MOMENTO_TEST_POSTGRES_DSN: postgres://postgres:ci@127.0.0.1:5432/momento?sslmode=disable
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v7
        with:
          go-version-file: go.mod
          cache: true
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: |
            web/package-lock.json
            sdk/package-lock.json
      # The reports answer by running their independent reads at the same time, so
      # the handlers that build them share variables across goroutines. The race
      # detector is what says that sharing is correct; without it a report that
      # occasionally returned a half-filled answer would look like a flaky test.
      # It costs about ninety seconds here, because these tests wait on a database
      # rather than on the CPU.
      - run: go test -race ./cmd/... ./internal/...
      - run: go vet ./cmd/... ./internal/...
      - run: go run golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest ./cmd/... ./internal/...
      - run: npm ci && npm audit && npm run typecheck && npm test && npm run build
        working-directory: sdk
      - run: npm ci && npm audit && npm run lint && npm test && npm run build
        working-directory: web
      - name: Build production image
        run: docker build --build-arg VERSION=ci --build-arg COMMIT=${GITHUB_SHA::12} -t momento:ci .
.PHONY: test build dev docker release-image

# internal/version holds the one declaration of what this tree is; a build that
# names no version reports that rather than a placeholder.
DECLARED_VERSION := $(shell sed -n 's/^[[:space:]]*Version[[:space:]]*=[[:space:]]*"\(.*\)"$$/\1/p' internal/version/version.go)
VERSION ?= $(DECLARED_VERSION)
COMMIT ?= $(shell git rev-parse --short HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)
BUILD_TIME ?= $(shell date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
RELEASE_VERSION := $(patsubst v%,%,$(VERSION))

# The service names itself the same way in both places it is named, and they are
# not the same shape because they are not the same kind of name: an image is a
# repository and a tag, a file is one word. VERSION may be given either as
# 0.34.2 or v0.34.2, so the v is added here rather than assumed to be there.
#   image    momento:v0.34.2
#   archive  momento-v0.34.2.tar.gz
IMAGE := momento:v$(RELEASE_VERSION)
ARCHIVE_NAME := momento-v$(RELEASE_VERSION)

test:
	go test ./cmd/... ./internal/...
	go vet ./cmd/... ./internal/...
	cd sdk && npm run typecheck && npm test
	cd web && npm run lint && npm test && npm run build

build:
	cd sdk && npm run build
	mkdir -p web/public
	cp sdk/dist/tracker.js web/public/tracker.js
	cd web && npm run build
	go build -trimpath -ldflags="-X github.com/hkjang/Momento/internal/version.Version=$(VERSION) -X github.com/hkjang/Momento/internal/version.Commit=$(COMMIT) -X github.com/hkjang/Momento/internal/version.BuildTime=$(BUILD_TIME)" -o bin/momento ./cmd/momento

dev:
	docker compose up --build

docker:
	docker build --build-arg VERSION=$(VERSION) --build-arg COMMIT=$(COMMIT) --build-arg BUILD_TIME=$(BUILD_TIME) -t $(IMAGE) .

release-image:
	docker build --build-arg VERSION=$(RELEASE_VERSION) --build-arg COMMIT=$(COMMIT) --build-arg BUILD_TIME=$(BUILD_TIME) -t $(IMAGE) .
	docker save $(IMAGE) | gzip -9 > $(ARCHIVE_NAME).tar.gz
	sha256sum $(ARCHIVE_NAME).tar.gz > $(ARCHIVE_NAME).tar.gz.sha256
